subject: english-literature
title: An Inspector Calls Stretch
welcome_lead: Stretch: was Goole a ghost, a policeman, or Priestley himself with a megaphone?
meta_desc: GCSE English Literature — essay-level analysis of Inspector Goole's identity and Priestley's politics.
final_note: You explored Goole as supernatural, allegorical and political — and Priestley's 1945 socialist agenda.

concepts.def: A story where characters stand for ideas
System where the state supports the poor and sick
1942 plan for UK welfare adopted after WW2
A character voicing the author's view

walkthroughs.body_html:
Clues suggest yes: 'Goole' = ghoul; he knows everything; the phone call reveals no real inspector exists.

His exit precedes a second phone call announcing a real death — as if he was the future warning the present. Ambiguity is deliberate.

Priestley was a socialist. The Inspector's lines are essentially his manifesto.

'If men will not learn that lesson, then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish' — Priestley's 1945 audience had just lived this. The play's polemical punch lands hard.

The phone rings; a real inspector is on his way. The play loops.

This cyclical structure argues that nothing changes for those who refuse to learn (Birlings senior); but Sheila and Eric have. The audience must choose which group they belong to.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
Dramatic irony is when something ironic happens in a play.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension between the character's words/actions and the audience's understanding.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a metaphor and a simile?
options: Metaphors are short and similes are long.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing IS another, making an implicit comparison without those connectives.
